catalog_locator: §2.2.4 'Stress placement', pp.33-38 (rule statement p.33, foot rules pp.34-35, caveat p.38); §2.1.4 p.24 (phonemic vs phonetic long vowels)
catalog_quote: Stress placement in Wambaya is sensitive to morphological structure; each polysyllabic morpheme constitutes a new domain for the placement of stress. Generally stress falls on the first syllable of the stress domain and on each following alternate syllable, except that the final syllable usually does not carry any stress. Stress placement is also sensitive to syllable weight as heavy syllables (i.e. those containing a phonemic long vowel) are always stressed whether they are in the first or second syllable of the stress domain (the only two positional possibilities for long vowels). Therefore, with the exception of a handful of words with a phonemic long vowel in their second syllable, primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word. (p.33) ... Phonemic long vowels always receive primary stress irrespective of their position in the word ... Long vowels as in (a) to (d) above howe…

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the standard reference grammar (Nordlinger 1998, PL C-140), which we hold; every segment of the deciding quotation was confirmed verbatim at the cited pages (p.33 rule statement, p.24 phonemic long vowels always primary-stressed, p.35 rule (iii), p.38 caveat). The coding (weight-sensitive, left edge, heavy = CVV with phonemic long vowel only, morpheme-based stress domains) matches the source exactly, including the author's own hedge that the analysis is provisional. sources.quote: 'Stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word-unit. There are few exceptions. With the addition of suffixes to a stem, stress moves to the penultimate vowel of the series of suffixes' (examples given are Djingili/Jingulu, not Wambaya). A family-level generalization in a 60-pp outline; Nordlinger 1998:33 fn.23 explicitly disagrees for Wambaya on the basis of her own fieldwork.

sources.quote: Comparative-historical only: marks primary stress with acute accent in reconstructions and cites Wambaya ng-ámany / k-ámany '1SG/3SG-come-PP' with stress on the first root vowel after a consonantal prefix; discusses diachronic stress shift to prefixes in Mirndi. No synchronic statement of the Wambaya word-stress rule or of long-vowel weight.

sources.note: The earlier description Nordlinger 1998:33 fn.23 names as conflicting (penultimate stress, p.17); holding it would document exactly what Chadwick claimed for Wambaya as opposed to Jingulu. Its published outline (Chadwick 1979, fetched sources) already shows the claim is a family-level generalization illustrated with Jingulu, so this would not change the coding.
